prohibited_recommendations: Do not start antiepileptic drugs based on convulsive syncope
Do not give further AV-nodal blockers (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, digoxin)
Do not perform lumbar puncture; no indication
Do not discharge home before pacing plan and clearance
Do not allow driving until pacemaker implant and physician clearance
required_recommendations: Recognise trifascicular block as a high-risk ECG pattern requiring inpatient monitoring
Identify convulsive movements as syncope rather than epilepsy

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical features of meningitis or encephalopathy.

accepted: Cardiac syncope due to paroxysmal high-grade AV block on a background of trifascicular conduction disease

differential.key_features: Structural heart disease and PVC burden raise concern for VT; must be excluded by monitoring and EP study.
Baseline bradycardia could be SA-node disease; SNRT and atrial pacing on EP study clarify.
Brief jerks (~5-15 s), no post-ictal confusion, no tongue bite, normal EEG — convulsive syncope rather than epilepsy.
On multiple antihypertensives including HCTZ but episodes not positional and tilt-table negative.
No clear trigger or prodrome, age and ECG argue against vasovagal etiology.

key_clinical_evidence: Bifascicular plus first-degree AV block constitutes trifascicular disease with high risk of progression to complete heart block
Convulsive syncope can mimic seizure — clinical features and ECG distinguish
Thiazide-induced electrolyte loss aggravates conduction-system disease
Paroxysmal high-grade block can be missed on a single ECG; prolonged monitoring is essential
OSA contributes to nocturnal bradyarrhythmia and must be addressed concurrently

clinical_pearls: Convulsive syncope occurs in up to 12% of syncopal episodes and is often misdiagnosed as epilepsy, leading to inappropriate antiepileptic drug treatment
Trifascicular block (bifascicular block plus first-degree AV block) with syncope carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block and is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker
The ECG in cardiac syncope may not capture the culprit arrhythmia at the time of presentation; the resting ECG findings of conduction disease provide critical diagnostic clues
Thiazide diuretics can cause electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) that exacerbate cardiac conduction abnormalities

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Williams is a 71-year-old man with a history of hypertension on multiple medications, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and obstructive sleep apnea who presents to the emergency department after a third episode of sudden loss of consciousness in six weeks. Today's episode occurred while he was sitting in a chair watching television at approximately 2:30 PM. His wife, who was in the room, reports that he suddenly became unresponsive and slumped to the left, falling out of the chair onto the floor. She observed brief jerking movements of both arms and legs lasting approximately 10 to 15 seconds. She describes his face as looking ashen gray during the episode. She called 911 and by the time she returned to his side approximately 30 seconds later, he was already waking up and asking what happened. She states he was fully alert and conversational within one minute of the event. There was no preceding cry, no tonic stiffening, no eye deviation, and no frothing at the mouth. She did not notice any tongue biting or urinary incontinence. The previous two episodes occurred three weeks ago and five weeks ago, respectively. The first episode happened while he was standing in line at the grocery store and was initially attributed to 'orthostatic hypotension' by his primary care physician, who reduced his hydrochlorothiazide dose. The second episode occurred while seated at the dinner table, and his wife again witnessed brief limb jerking for several seconds. He was referred to neurology for concern of new-onset seizures but the appointment was not for another two weeks. He has also noticed intermittent lightheadedness and a sensation of his heart 'pausing' or 'skipping' over the past two months, particularly when climbing stairs. He denies chest pain, sustained palpitations, shortness of breath at rest, or exertional dyspnea beyond his baseline. He denies any prior seizure history, head trauma, or family history of epilepsy. He has no history of aura, tongue biting, prolonged confusion, or prolonged shaking episodes.
